newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania farming, energy reform key for new loans - IMF.
newsitem.headline: Romania farming, energy reform key for new loans - IMF.

text.p: Reforms of Romania's farming and energy-intensive sectors are crucial to stabilise the country's economy and to secure loans worth over $1.0 billion from international lenders, an IMF official said on Monday.

"Emphasis on early reform of these sectors could bring the deficit down to something that can be financed without creating inflationary pressures," International Monetary Fund mission chief Poul Thomsen told Reuters.

Thomsen was speaking shortly after Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea announced a radical reform package agreed with international lenders, including the IMF, underpinning new loans worth over $1.0 billion needed to prop up the economy.
Of this, the Fund might disburse more than $400 million, after an IMF board meeting in Washington due in April endorsed Ciorbea's reforms package.
"If approved, the $400 million or so would be disbursed in five tranches over one year," Thomsen said.
Thomsen said conclusion of talks on the new loan accord after only five weeks was a "positive record."
"The Fund has definitely sent a signal. This government is serious about the reform and the IMF is capable of moving fast," he said.

The IMF and World Bank withheld loans to Romania in 1996 on grounds that the former leftist government, ousted in elections last November, had stalled reforms, imposed foreign exchange market curbs and overspent public money.
"Our experience with Romania in the past is that again and again stabilisation plans have broken down," Thomsen said.

Ciorbea's reformist government pledged radical surgery in key economic sectors, to cut communist-era subsidies and put the economy on a free-market footing along with steps to ensure social protection to the needy.

"The programme is very strong on liberalisation of prices. We very much welcome its ambitious targets for reform, restructuring, privatisation and closure of unviable entities. This is the hard part of the programme," Thomsen said.

Thomsen said that he did not expect social unrest to follow restructuring of huge state-run companies. Officials expect the move to push unemployment to some 8.0 percent, up from 6.0 percent at present.
"There is no doubt the programme for restructuring will entail considerable social costs," Thomsen said.
"But a fundamental element in this programme that lends it credibility is the mobilisation of 2.3 percent more of budget resources for social programmes. This is actually a lot of money," he said.
